subject: chopperMotorbike
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: custom chopper motorbike.
Style: Overwatch.
reasoning:
I'm picturing a custom chopper motorbike rendered in Overwatch's stylized aesthetic—bold shapes, orange/blue accents, emblem decals—with a long front fork, big rear tire, V-twin engine, and ape-hanger handlebars.

I'm thinking through the rigging structure too: since this is a vehicle rather than a creature, I'll need a root joint for the builder requirement, plus additional joints for the wheels and steering fork to allow proper articulation. Now I'm working out exact proportions and placement—overall length around 2.4m, wheel radii sized differently for that raked chopper look, with the rear wheel set back and the front wheel positioned forward along a steeply angled fork, and planning to construct the tires using torus geometry.

Writing tire profile coordinates...

Lathe takes a bone option with centered position and 20 segments. For the wheel rim and spokes, I'm considering building spoked wheels manually with trig loops in the YZ plane, generating rods from hub to rim points at 16 spokes per wheel, going for a stylized Overwatch-like disc wheel look.

Actually simplifying to a chunkier mag wheel with 5 thick spokes plus a glowing torus accent ring on the side using emissive cyan/orange materials. For the palette, I'm leaning into Overwatch-style saturated colors—orange and dark navy/blue—for the bike's body paint and accents.

For the actual paint job, I'll avoid any trademarked logos and design my own hex-and-chevron emblem instead. Rather than a flat toon/cel shader, I'll write a custom shading helper that blends warm tones toward the top of surfaces and cooler blue tones toward the bottom based on surface normal, giving a hand-painted gradient look with some edge wear for grit.

Now I'm checking what the kit module exports — paint utilities like mix, rgb, noise, and smoothstep all live in one module, and I can pull mechanical kit pieces like metal presets and a gearTrain decal generator for steel/copper trim. I'm considering adding a small flat-style gear cluster decal to the engine cover for mechanical flavor, working out the tooth count, module size, and bone attachment needed to make it fit properly.

I'm now laying out the chopper's geometry in meters — placing rear and front wheel centers, setting tire radii and widths, defining a 2.0m wheelbase, and positioning the steering head and fork rake angle for an extreme chopper-style frame geometry.

Then I'm sketching the skeleton structure: a root "frame" joint, a "rearWheel" hinge joint, a "steer" joint at the head aimed along the fork toward the front axle, a "frontWheel" joint as its child, plus kickstand and handlebar joints, working out naming and hierarchy for each part.

Since bones run between joints automatically unless specified, I'll explicitly set `bone:` every time to avoid ambiguity, and define a small helper wrapping b.part with that default. I'll lean on world-space positions plus dir/aim rather than relative local bone math since orientation conventions are tricky here.

For orientation I'll use explicit bone and model-space `at`, combined with dir/axis, defaulting cylinder axis to y and keeping box rotation simple. I'm sketching a `rodTo` helper that wraps b.rod for connecting two points with a radius and color, and noting that sides can be lowered to 6 for a chunkier, low-poly look instead of the default 8. For frame tubes I'm planning to use catmull sweep paths bound to the frame joint, starting the main backbone pipe near the head and running it back along the top.

Now I'm working out piece placement, starting with the base platform as a low hexagonal cylinder, and figuring out ground offset math so the bike's lowest points touch y=0 -- settling on a constant GROUND value added to all bike coordinates to keep things consistent.

With a vertex pointing toward +Z, that aligns with front/back orientation. Checking bike length: rear tire extends to about -1.22, front tire to about 1.58, giving a total span near 2.8 centered around 0.18, so a hex radius of 1.9 should comfortably cover the whole bike.

Rethinking proportions though - the hex width across flats is bigger than I need for a 0.9-wide bike, so I'm shortening the chopper layout (rear at -0.75, front at 1.1, head at 0.55) and recentering the base around z=0.15 with a tighter radius of 1.6, giving a hex width of about 2.77. I'll build this as a stacked hex platform with an orange trim ring around the edge and a slightly raised dark inner deck carrying an emblem decal, finished off with some stylized orange chevron markings.

For props I'm keeping things minimal but thematic -- a toolbox, a jerrycan, a traffic cone, a small crate stack, and scattered bolts, plus a glowing holographic emblem decal on the base to sell that Junkertown/Route 66 vibe without overloading the scene. Now I'm listing out the wheel components: lathe-built tire with painted tread, chrome rim, hub cap, six spoke rods, glow rings on both sides, a thin steel brake disc, a caliper box, and a fender.

For the fenders I'm working out swept geometry over the tire arcs -- using box-section sweeps along curved paths computed with trig, where the path's orientation keeps widths running along world X so the fender wraps naturally over the wheel. The rear fender path sweeps from the lower-rear angle up over the top of the tire using the wheel's radius to position each point.

For the fork, I'm defining paired stanchion rods per side running from the triple tree at the head down to the axle, splitting into thicker chrome uppers and thinner slider lowers, with the fork direction computed from the head-to-axle vector, and I'm adding a steering neck tube aimed from the head joint toward the front axle.

Working backward from the axle, the triple tree point lands near (0, 1.0, 0.576), which sets the top of the fork assembly along the steering axis.

Still estimating head tube height (around y=1.14) and the chopper's ape-hanger handlebars, sketching grip positions and riser clamp coordinates for the sweeping bar curve.

Now I'm positioning the headlight, placing a round bucket shape ahead of the fork tubes by offsetting forward and slightly up from the fork's reference point.

For the paint job, I'm planning a deep blue base with orange-to-yellow flame tongues licking backward along the sides, using a zigzag boundary function based on z-position to create the flame tips.
